design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory study with an active comparison drug, at the Human Behavioral Pharmacology Laboratory, University of Chicago. 21 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 38 who had used ecstasy or MDMA at least twice each had four sessions, in randomized order and at least 5 days apart, receiving one opaque capsule per session: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg (a fixed dose, not adjusted for body weight) or placebo (study conditions). Self-ratings: a 15-item visual analogue scale (VAS) at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 210 and 240 minutes and the 72-item Profile of Mood States (POMS) at 0, 90 and 240 minutes; five outcomes chosen from the hypotheses (VAS sociable, playful, loving and lonely; POMS friendliness), each analysed as peak change from baseline. Emotion-recognition tasks from 65 minutes after the capsule, once per session: a facial emotion recognition task (FER; Ekman faces morphed from neutral to full expression in 10% steps, shown for 500 ms; anger, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral; 170 pictures), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes test (36 items) and the DANVA-2 adult paralanguage test (24 voice clips). Repeated-measures analyses of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted follow-up tests. Participants sat alone in testing rooms with contact only with a research assistant. The PDF read is the NIH Public Access author manuscript (accepted version, pages 1 to 14), not the version of record (Biol Psychiatry 68:1134-1140); anchors cite the manuscript's own page numbers (PDF p.).
can_establish: Whether, in 21 healthy young adults with limited earlier ecstasy use, tested alone in a laboratory, these MDMA doses changed self-rated loving, friendly, playful, lonely and sociable feelings and the accuracy of recognising emotions in briefly shown faces, in eye regions and in voices, compared with placebo and with methamphetamine 20 mg.
cannot_establish: What MDMA does to empathy or social behaviour with real people (participants were alone and the tasks used pictures and recorded voices); whether the loving and friendly feelings are specific to MDMA (after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg they did not differ significantly from those after methamphetamine); effects at other amounts, after repeated doses or in people who had never taken MDMA; or the size of the self-rated effects in natural units (their means appear only in small figures and the VAS range is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: internet advertisements and word of mouth; healthy volunteers aged 18 to 38 who reported using MDMA or ecstasy on at least two occasions (PDF p. 3, Methods and Materials > Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded after screening (medical examination, electrocardiogram, structured clinical interview): DSM-IV Axis I psychiatric disorder including substance dependence; signs of medical or neurological illness; body mass index outside 18.5 to 30; cardiovascular illness in a first-degree relative; prior adverse response to ecstasy; pregnancy or lactation (PDF p. 3). Before each session: no cannabis for 7 days, no alcohol or medications for 24 hours and no other recreational drugs (for example ecstasy) for 48 hours, checked with urine, saliva and breath tests; pregnancy test for women at every session (PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.4 (SD 4.9); 9 of 21 women; 17 Caucasian, 2 Asian, 1 African-American, 1 mixed race. First ecstasy use at mean age 19.8 (SD 2.7); lifetime ecstasy use on a mean of 15.0 occasions (SD 23.1), 13 participants fewer than 10 times. In the past month 12 smoked cigarettes at least weekly, all drank alcohol and 16 used cannabis; lifetime, all had used cannabis, all but 2 stimulants such as cocaine and all but 1 hallucinogens (PDF p. 5, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: No withdrawals are reported. The self-rating analyses had 20 participants ('missing data', reason not given, Figure 1 and 2 legends, PDF pp. 11-12) and the voice task 20 (equipment malfunction, Table 1 footnote, PDF pp. 13-14); whether the same person is missing from both is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: People with earlier ecstasy experience who answered advertisements or heard by word of mouth and passed a health and psychiatric screen; people with psychiatric disorders, drug dependence or an earlier bad reaction to ecstasy are absent by design. Prior experience was required for ethical reasons, and the authors say the findings may not generalize to people new to MDMA, while noting they recruited people with limited prior use (PDF p. 7). Most also used cannabis, alcohol and other drugs.

exposure.measurement: Drugs given in the laboratory in opaque size-00 gelatin capsules: MDMA or methamphetamine with lactose or dextrose filler, or filler only for placebo (PDF p. 3). The source and purity of the study drugs are not stated in the manuscript, and no plasma drug levels are reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral capsule per session of MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg or placebo, in randomized order, sessions at least 5 days apart, starting at noon after 2 hours without food; tasks from 65 minutes after the capsule; participants stayed in the laboratory at least 4.5 hours and until drug effects had passed (PDF pp. 3-4). The authors describe the MDMA doses as low to moderate and 1.5 mg/kg as within recreational ranges, citing other papers (PDF p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was common (see demographics). Use before sessions was limited by the abstinence rules above, checked by urine (QuickTox), saliva (Oratect III) and breath alcohol screens (PDF p. 3); drug-use history was not used in any analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Cannabis 7 days, alcohol and medications 24 hours, other recreational drugs 48 hours before each session, with urine, saliva and breath screens (PDF p. 3).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own placebo session (within person), and methamphetamine 20 mg as an active stimulant comparison, included to test whether effects are specific to MDMA (PDF p. 2).
comparison.matching: Within person; capsules given in randomized order. The authors report that session order had no significant effect in any analysis and was dropped from the models (no statistics printed, PDF p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (within-person design). Trait sociability, which the authors suggest may shape the response (PDF p. 7), was not measured; expectation was assessed only through participants' guesses of the drug received.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within person); the same abstinence rules applied before every session.

outcomes.instruments: VAS of 15 adjectives (stimulated, bored, sedated, anxious, insightful, nauseated, loving, dizzy, sociable, confused, lonely, elated, playful, blank, restless); POMS (72 adjectives rated 0 to 4, 8 subscales including friendliness, the mean of 8 items); FER (proportion correct per emotion and number of emotional faces misclassified as neutral); Reading the Mind in the Eyes test, revised (36 items, total correct); DANVA-2 adult paralanguage test (24 clips of one neutral sentence spoken happily, sadly, angrily or fearfully at two intensities; total correct) (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established tasks cited to their sources; the FER is described as sensitive to serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and the Eyes test to oxytocin (PDF p. 4). The range of the VAS is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Prosocial feelings as single VAS items and the POMS friendliness subscale, each as peak change from the pre-capsule baseline; emotion recognition as accuracy. Empathy itself was not measured: the authors treat identifying others' emotions as a first step of empathy (PDF p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise follow-ups for the self-ratings; for the FER, simple main effects at 0.05 divided by the number of emotion categories, then pairwise tests adjusted for the total number of analyses (PDF pp. 4-5). No correction across the 5 self-rating outcomes or the 3 tasks; the analysis of faces misclassified as neutral is exploratory and uncorrected (PDF p. 6). Editors' count of 13 outcomes: 5 self-ratings, FER accuracy for 5 categories, FER misclassifications as neutral, Eyes total and DANVA-2 total.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind, with four possible drugs. Outcomes are self-ratings and computer tasks. Six of 21 participants guessed ecstasy when they had received methamphetamine; how drug guesses were collected and how often MDMA was correctly identified are not reported (PDF p. 6).

analysis.effect_sizes: Self-ratings, n = 20 (parametric results reported because non-parametric tests agreed, except for VAS lonely): VAS loving F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004, eta squared 0.21 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo); POMS friendliness F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001, eta squared 0.26 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and above MDMA 0.75 mg/kg); VAS lonely, Friedman chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008, r = 0.54 (MDMA 0.75 mg/kg above methamphetamine and placebo); VAS playful F(3,57) = 8.57, p < 0.001, eta squared 0.31 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and MDMA 0.75 mg/kg; methamphetamine above placebo); VAS sociable F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05, eta squared 0.14 (methamphetamine above placebo only) (PDF pp. 5-6). Loving and friendliness after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from methamphetamine (PDF p. 6). Means are shown only in Figures 1 and 2 (PDF pp. 11-12), low-resolution images read approximately (embedded images enlarged): largest mean change in VAS loving about 0.27 at 120 minutes after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, about 0.15 after methamphetamine and about 0 after placebo; POMS friendliness about 0.68 at 90 minutes after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, about 0.35 after methamphetamine, about 0.03 after placebo and about -0.19 after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg (POMS items are rated 0 to 4; the VAS range is not stated). Emotion recognition, n = 21: FER drug by emotion interaction F(5.2,104.6) = 3.23, p = 0.008; fear F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18; proportion of fearful faces correctly named 0.63 (SD 0.07) after placebo, 0.59 (0.12) after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, 0.55 (0.10) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and 0.59 (0.10) after methamphetamine; placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg t(20) = 3.94, significant after Bonferroni correction; placebo against methamphetamine t(20) = 2.59 and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against methamphetamine t(20) = 1.31, not significant (Table 1, PDF p. 13). Editors' calculation: within-person standardized difference for fear, placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, dz = 3.94 divided by the square root of 21, about 0.86; mean difference 0.08 (95% CI about 0.04 to 0.12, from the printed t and the rounded means). Other facial emotions did not change after correction (happiness F = 0.96, sadness 3.60, anger 2.0, neutral 2.84; df 3,60). Emotional faces misclassified as neutral: 44.90 (SD 11.31) after placebo against 51.71 (10.58) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, overall F(3,60) = 3.25 and t(20) = 2.52, each p < 0.05 uncorrected (exploratory). Eyes test total 26.81 (5.14) placebo, 26.10 (2.70) MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, F(3,60) = 0.58; DANVA-2 total 18.05 (1.70) placebo, 17.20 (2.19) MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 18.70 (2.11) methamphetamine, F(3,57) = 3.01 (Table 1, PDF p. 13).
analysis.covariates: None. Session order was tested and dropped (no statistics). The methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight; post hoc, only methamphetamine's effect on playfulness correlated with body weight (r = -0.45, p = 0.04) (PDF p. 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or published protocol is mentioned in the manuscript; the five self-rating outcomes are described as chosen from the study hypotheses (PDF p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 5 of the 15 VAS items and 1 of the 8 POMS subscales are reported. Cardiovascular measures taken at baseline and throughout every session are not reported (PDF p. 3). Means and SDs of the self-ratings are not printed (figures only), and the drug-guess data are summarized in two sentences (PDF p. 6).
analysis.power: No power calculation; 21 participants (20 for self-ratings and the voice task). Non-significant results (other facial emotions, the Eyes test, voices, MDMA against methamphetamine) are imprecise and do not show that no effect exists.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 21 healthy young adults with some earlier ecstasy use, tested alone, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg raised self-rated loving and friendliness against placebo but not significantly against methamphetamine 20 mg; only methamphetamine significantly raised self-rated sociability; both MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and methamphetamine raised playfulness; MDMA 0.75 mg/kg raised loneliness. MDMA 1.5 mg/kg lowered the proportion of fearful faces correctly named from 0.63 to 0.55 (the one emotion out of five that passed correction) and did not detectably change recognition of other facial emotions, of complex emotions from the eyes or of emotions in voices; its effect on fear recognition did not differ significantly from methamphetamine's.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say MDMA increased 'empathogenic' feelings and robustly reduced recognition of fearful faces, findings described as consistent with increased social approach rather than empathy, and call this the first published demonstration of an overt behavioral effect of MDMA in humans (PDF pp. 1, 6). The abstract does not say that the loving and friendly ratings after MDMA did not differ from those after methamphetamine, which the Discussion acknowledges, concluding that MDMA's prosocial effects may be less selective than believed (PDF pp. 6-7). The Discussion adds that ecstasy, while increasing feelings of connection, "can subtly impair interpersonal competence" and may increase social risk-taking, and suggests that reduced fear perception may help MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (PDF pp. 7-8); neither was tested. The statement that expectancy played a minor role rests on a non-significant re-analysis by drug guess in 21 people (PDF p. 6).

timeline.event: Same laboratory, fMRI study: as described here, MDMA altered neural responses to social material but did not change the accuracy of identifying emotions in facial pictures (PDF p. 2).

Hysek and colleagues (Basel), 32 volunteers, MDMA 125 mg against placebo: lower accuracy for fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised dynamic faces, not for happy faces; they cite this paper as consistent, and also cite it for raised self-rated sociability, which this paper did not find for MDMA (only methamphetamine raised sociability significantly).

replication.where_it_stands: Lower recognition of fear in faces after MDMA has been found in two placebo-controlled laboratory studies from different groups (this one, with static faces, and Hysek et al., 2014, with dynamic faces and other negative emotions as well). Whether the loving and friendly feelings are specific to MDMA rather than shared with stimulants rests on this study's comparison with methamphetamine, which found no significant difference either way.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse (DA02812) (Acknowledgments, PDF p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest or financial-disclosure statement appears in the author manuscript read; the version of record was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Human Behavioral Pharmacology Laboratory, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, University of Chicago; the first author also New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (PDF p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A larger, preregistered placebo-controlled study in which people interact with real partners (for example, conversations scored for how accurately each reads the other's feelings), with more than one MDMA dose, a stimulant comparison sized to detect a difference from MDMA, plasma drug levels and a reported check of blinding.

domains.note: Capsules given in randomized order; how the order was generated or balanced is not described (PDF p. 3).
Sessions at least 5 days apart to allow drug elimination; session order reported to have no effect in any analysis (no statistics).

Double blind with opaque capsules and four possible drugs, but 6 of 21 guessed ecstasy on methamphetamine; how guesses were collected and how often MDMA was identified are not reported; the re-analysis by guess was non-significant in 21 people.
One participant missing from the self-rating analyses (reason not given) and one from the voice task (equipment malfunction); otherwise complete.
Self-ratings can be shaped by recognising the drug; the computer tasks are objective; the VAS range is not stated.
No registration; 5 of 15 VAS items and 1 of 8 POMS subscales reported (chosen from stated hypotheses); cardiovascular data not reported; the DANVA-2 F(3,57) = 3.01 is printed without its corrected p.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person study with an active comparison drug; the concerns are the undescribed randomization, partial blinding and selective reporting of the subjective scales, none of which is likely to reverse the main findings. The source may be cited for higher self-rated loving and friendliness after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg than after placebo, but not higher than after methamphetamine 20 mg; for lower accuracy in naming fearful faces after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (0.55 against 0.63 after placebo); and for no detectable change in recognising other facial emotions, eye-region emotions or vocal emotions in 21 people. It should not be cited for effects on empathy or behaviour towards real people, for the feelings being specific to MDMA, or for other doses.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 21 healthy volunteers (9 women) aged 18 to 38, mean 24.4 (SD 4.9), who had used ecstasy at least twice (mean 15.0 lifetime occasions; 13 fewer than 10) each had four double-blind sessions in randomized order, at least 5 days apart: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg and placebo (study conditions).
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Participants, 1st paragraph and Experimental Protocol, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg raised self-rated loving (VAS; F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004, eta squared 0.21) and POMS friendliness (F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001, eta squared 0.26) against placebo; friendliness was also higher than after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg; n = 20.

The loving and friendliness ratings after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from those after methamphetamine 20 mg; only methamphetamine significantly raised self-rated sociability (F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05, eta squared 0.14; methamphetamine above placebo); MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and methamphetamine both raised playfulness (F(3,57) = 8.57, p < 0.001, eta squared 0.31).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph and 3rd paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); Figure 2 (PDF p. 12)
key_findings.note: Read approximately from the low-resolution Figure 2: the mean sociability curve after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (peak about 0.26 at 120 minutes) is as high as methamphetamine's (about 0.22); the analysis used each person's peak change, and only methamphetamine's difference from placebo passed the Bonferroni-adjusted test.

key_findings.finding: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg raised self-rated loneliness against methamphetamine and placebo (Friedman chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008, r = 0.54).

Fear recognition: the proportion of fearful faces correctly named was 0.63 (SD 0.07) after placebo and 0.55 (SD 0.10) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (t(20) = 3.94, significant after Bonferroni correction; drug effect on fear F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18); it was 0.59 after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 0.59 after methamphetamine, and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from methamphetamine (t(20) = 1.31).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dz about 0.86 (3.94 divided by the square root of 21); a fall of 8 percentage points, about 3 of the 40 fearful faces.

key_findings.finding: No significant change after correction in recognising happy, sad, angry or neutral faces (F(3,60) = 0.96, 3.60, 2.0 and 2.84), complex emotions from the eye region (Eyes test total 26.81 after placebo, 26.10 after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg; F(3,60) = 0.58) or emotions in voices (DANVA-2, F(3,57) = 3.01; n = 20); no drug by emotion interaction for voices.
key_findings.note: With the uncorrected degrees of freedom printed, DANVA-2 F(3,57) = 3.01 corresponds to p of about 0.04 (editors' calculation); the paper reports no effect, presumably after the sphericity correction it describes, but prints neither the corrected degrees of freedom nor p.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg increased the number of emotional faces misclassified as neutral (mean 51.71, SD 10.58, against 44.90, SD 11.31, after placebo; t(20) = 2.52, p < 0.05 uncorrected).

Expectancy: 6 of 21 participants guessed they had taken ecstasy when they had received methamphetamine; a re-analysis by the drug each participant thought they had received found no significant relation with any measure that was sensitive to the drugs.
Setting: participants were alone in testing rooms, their only social contact a research assistant told not to interact beyond the protocol, without telephone or internet access.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Experimental Protocol, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: static face photographs may be less ecologically valid than dynamic stimuli; no task compared social with non-social stimuli; the methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight (only methamphetamine's playfulness effect correlated with weight, r = -0.45, p = 0.04); all participants had earlier ecstasy experience, so findings may not generalize to people new to MDMA.

Authors' interpretation: the pattern may be more consistent with increased social approach (sociability) than with increased empathy; MDMA may ease social interaction by reducing the impact of others' negative emotions rather than by improving recognition of, or sensitivity to, them. (The cited Discussion paragraph hedges with 'may be'; only the abstract states it without the hedge.)

reporting_issues.issue: Voice task: Table 1 prints the drug effect on DANVA-2 as F(3,57) = 3.01 without a significance mark; with these uncorrected degrees of freedom p is about 0.04 (editors' calculation). The text says MDMA did not affect DANVA-2 accuracy, and the corrected degrees of freedom and p (the paper interprets Huynh-Feldt or Greenhouse-Geisser corrected levels) are not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null result for voices may be borderline rather than clearly absent; the lowest mean was after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (17.20) and the highest after methamphetamine (18.70).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (N = 21) and the Results (9 of the 21 female; 6 of 21 guessed) give 21 participants, but the self-rating analyses (figure legends) and the voice task (Table 1 footnote, p. 14) have 20, without saying who is missing; Table 1 prints uncorrected degrees of freedom (3,60) for the fear effect while the text gives the corrected F(2.8,56.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the degrees of freedom printed in the text fit n = 20 for the self-ratings and n = 21 for the face task. (The main Methods section gives no N.)

reporting_issues.issue: The effect size for loneliness is given as r = 0.54 alongside a four-condition Friedman test; how r was derived is not stated. The range of the VAS is not stated, and the figures show mean changes of at most about 0.3 units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the self-rated effects cannot be expressed in standard units from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiovascular measures were taken at baseline and regularly during every session but are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: No physiological or safety data from these sessions can be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 40, cited for methamphetamine being associated with social and particularly sexual enhancement in some subcultures, is a study of MDMA neurotoxicity in neonatal rats (Meyer et al., 2004). The statement that empathogenic effects are a motivation for recreational use cites a rat study of oxytocin (reference 2) together with a study of ecstasy experiences (reference 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The methamphetamine statement is not supported by its citation in the manuscript, and the motivation statement rests on reference 3; the version of record was not checked for corrections.

disagreements.reviewer: Fear specificity: methamphetamine and MDMA 0.75 mg/kg both had a fear accuracy of 0.59; their comparisons with placebo (t(20) = 2.59 and 2.27) are not significant after Bonferroni correction but would be p of about 0.02 and 0.03 uncorrected (editors' calculation), so the fall in fear recognition is not shown to be specific to MDMA.
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.

disagreements.reviewer: Accuracy does not separate sensitivity from response bias: after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, neutral faces were named correctly more often (0.77 against 0.69, not significant) while emotional faces were more often called neutral, consistent with a shift towards answering 'neutral' (Table 1).
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.
